title: The Settlement With Gaps
briefing: In 1555, after decades of religious war, the estates of the Holy Roman Empire met at Augsburg and agreed to disagree by law. The Peace of Augsburg brought Catholics and Lutherans together under one public peace and left each prince to set the religion of his own territory; subjects who would not conform were free only to sell their goods and leave. It was a settlement built to freeze a quarrel in place rather than to resolve it — and it said nothing at all about the Calvinists, whose numbers were quietly growing.
situation: The danger lay in the gaps. One clause, the Ecclesiastical Reservation, required that any bishop or abbot who turned Protestant surrender his lands so that they stayed Catholic — but the Lutherans had never accepted it, and went on installing Protestant administrators over church territories regardless. By the 1580s so many of these lands had slipped into Protestant hands that the Catholic majority in the imperial Diet itself was at risk. Each disputed abbey and bishopric had become a lawsuit waiting to turn into a war.
historian_note: Wilson treats Augsburg as part of the Empire's constitutional settlement rather than a simple pause in religious war. Its unresolved legal-confessional questions became usable political weapons once rulers and estates ceased trusting one another's interpretation.

options.label: Insist on the strict letter of the Reservation and move to recover the church lands.
options.consequence: Catholic prelates and the Bavarian court take heart, certain the law is at last on their side. The Protestant estates set their clerks to memorials of their own, warning that to enforce the Reservation against eighty years of practice would shatter the very peace it claims to protect.

options.label: Treat Augsburg as a living compact, its silences to be settled only by negotiation.
options.consequence: The crown is seen as the guardian of the settlement rather than the master of its ambiguities. The moderate estates keep their seats at the table, while Catholic reformers complain that churches and revenues are being signed away under the name of peace.

options.label: Leave the disputed lands as they stand until a concrete case forces a ruling.
options.consequence: No estate is made to retreat today, and the files stay open. In chapter houses and town councils, lawyers on both sides go on gathering their proofs for the quarrel everyone knows is coming.

title: Leagues of Protection
briefing: By 1608 the machinery for keeping the imperial peace had seized up: that year's Diet broke up without agreement for the first time in living memory, and the high court had stopped functioning. Despairing of the old institutions, the Protestant princes acted alone. Days after the Diet collapsed, a group led by the Palatinate met at Auhausen and swore a Protestant Union — a standing alliance of mutual defence, contribution, and aid. Fourteen months later the Catholic princes answered with a League of their own under Maximilian of Bavaria.
situation: Both alliances spoke the careful language of self-defence, not rebellion. Their charters promised only counsel, compensation, and aid in the hour of danger — yet each also named commanders, treasuries, and quotas, and claimed the right to march when the law moved too slowly. Neither would enrol more than half its confession; the great Lutheran elector of Saxony, distrusting the Calvinist Palatinate, stood aloof from both. For the first time the Empire was arming itself in two camps under cover of the public peace.
historian_note: Wilson stresses that the Union and Liga did not make war inevitable. They mattered because they turned insecurity into institutions and gave ambitious directors ways to spread costs, claim legitimacy, and mobilize support.

memory_variants.briefing: Coming so soon after the crown pressed the strict letter of Augsburg, the news from Auhausen reads like a direct reply: the Palatinate and the Protestant estates now bind themselves to mutual aid before any court can weigh their danger. From Munich the Catholic princes answer with a League under Maximilian of Bavaria.
memory_variants.situation: The strict line lately taken at court has given the Catholic side confidence — and given the Protestants their argument that the ordinary remedies are no longer safe. Each alliance professes service to the public peace; each also names its commanders, treasuries, and quotas, and claims the right to march when delay threatens land and people.

memory_variants.briefing: The reports from Auhausen and Munich arrive as proof that consultation alone can no longer hold confessional fear inside the old institutions. The Palatinate and the Protestant estates have sealed a Protestant Union for mutual defence; from Munich the Catholic princes answer with a League under Maximilian of Bavaria.
memory_variants.situation: The court's earlier restraint keeps a language of moderation within reach, but it also makes the two leagues harder to condemn together. Each alliance professes service to the public peace; each also names its commanders, treasuries, and quotas, and claims the right to march when delay threatens land and people.

memory_variants.briefing: The reports from Auhausen and Munich arrive atop a growing file of unanswered petitions. The Palatinate and the Protestant estates have sealed a Protestant Union for mutual defence; from Munich the Catholic princes answer with a League under Maximilian of Bavaria.
memory_variants.situation: Leaving the disputed lands unjudged has spared the Empire a single provocation, but it has left every estate to measure its own danger. Each alliance professes service to the public peace; each also names its commanders, treasuries, and quotas, and claims the right to march when delay threatens land and people.

options.label: Tolerate the leagues as lawful insurance, so long as they stay within the public peace.
options.consequence: The alliances keep their language careful and go on professing obedience — while keeping their treasuries full and their soldiers ready, against the day imperial justice arrives too late.

options.label: Condemn both leagues as unlawful factions against the public peace.
options.consequence: The court speaks again in the old language of the Landfrieden. Union and League alike reply that their oaths were sworn in self-defence, and that it was the slowness of the imperial courts that drove them to it.

options.label: Welcome the Catholic League as the necessary answer to Protestant union.
options.consequence: The Catholic prelates write to Munich with new confidence, and Maximilian's direction becomes the natural channel of armed Catholic aid. The emperor gains a shield — but one held in another prince's hand.

title: A Royal Promise in Bohemia
briefing: In Bohemia the crown's weakness became the Protestants' opportunity. In 1609, with the ageing Emperor Rudolf locked in a ruinous struggle against his brother Matthias, the Protestant estates forced their way into his palace and wrung from him the Letter of Majesty — a charter granting the lords, knights, and royal towns the free choice of religion, the right to build churches and schools, and a standing committee of Defensors to guard these liberties. Among the militants who extracted it was Count Thurn, rewarded with the keepership of the crown jewels.
situation: The charter created, in effect, a Protestant government beside the Catholic one. Royal councillors at once began to read it narrowly — drawing distinctions over crown land, over church lordships, over the exact reach of its words. The estates answered that a promise entered among the kingdom's fundamental liberties could not be whittled away by officials without dissolving the obedience owed to the crown itself. Every clause had become a frontier.
historian_note: The Letter of Majesty makes the Bohemian crisis a dispute over recorded estate privileges as well as confession. Later enforcement could be presented as lawful correction by one side and charter-breaking by the other.

options.label: Uphold the Letter as a broad and binding charter of Bohemian liberty.
options.consequence: The Protestant estates take the answer as proof that obedience and chartered worship can stand together. The Catholic clergy see a written wall raised before any restoration in one of the chief kingdoms of the Habsburgs.

options.label: Read the Letter narrowly wherever crown and church rights are touched.
options.consequence: Royal officials proceed on a defensible distinction in law. The Defensors copy the same order into their book of grievances — proof, they say, that the charter is being emptied while its seal still hangs in plain view.

options.label: Give no ruling, and leave local practice to bear the strain.
options.consequence: No order forces a retreat this season. Parish priests and noble patrons, royal judges and elected Defensors, all go on acting upon rival readings of the same royal paper.

title: The Styrian Lesson
briefing: Long before Bohemia, there was Styria. As archduke of Inner Austria from 1596, the young Ferdinand inherited five provinces whose nobility and towns were overwhelmingly Lutheran — in Styria itself, only five noble families in 135 had stayed Catholic. Jesuit-educated and newly returned from a pilgrimage to Rome, he resolved to win them all back.
situation: He moved by method, not by mob. In 1598 he revived the reform commission, summoning the three Estates separately so they could not combine, and forcing a Catholic onto each governing committee. Where law would not serve, force did: officials were tortured into surrendering the Protestant school at Graz, an 800-man garrison guarded the commissioners, and Bishop Brenner — soon nicknamed the 'hammer of heretics' — toured the towns expelling pastors and teachers, closing schools, and demolishing churches, one of them blown up with gunpowder at Eisenerz. The Estates withheld taxes and threatened to emigrate; in the end most of them stayed and conformed. The lesson was dangerous precisely because it had worked.
historian_note: Wilson treats Inner Austria as the formative setting for Ferdinand's legalistic Catholic restoration before the Bohemian crisis.

options.label: Trust the Styrian method — legal commissions, Catholic appointments, and force where needed.
options.consequence: Ferdinand's confidence hardens into doctrine: restoration can be presented as obedience to law, not innovation. What worked in Graz, his advisers assure him, will work wherever the crown is strong enough.

options.label: Advance Catholicism quietly by patronage and appointment, sparing the public expulsions.
options.consequence: The recovery goes on, but without martyrs or spectacle. The zealous among his advisers ask whether such caution is not simply surrender dressed as prudence.

options.label: Seek a fresh compact with the Estates before reviving the commission.
options.consequence: The Estates gain a language of consent, and Ferdinand gains fewer enemies — and a conscience less certain that he has done his duty by God.

title: Before the Window
briefing: By 1617 Ferdinand had been accepted as king of Bohemia — only two delegates voted against him — and he had confirmed the Letter of Majesty, believing himself to be keeping it. His officials thought otherwise. They closed a Protestant church at Braunau and pulled another down at Klostergrab, arguing that the charter did not cover worship on Catholic-owned land; they arrested the petitioners who complained, and set royal judges over the parishes' funds.
situation: To Count Thurn and the Defensors, these were not isolated cases but the charter being dismantled clause by clause — and Thurn had a grievance of his own, for Ferdinand had stripped him of the keepership of the crown jewels. Every royal answer now bore on the reign to come. The Catholic councillors urged firmness and the vindication of royal rights; the Protestant defenders warned that arrests and demolitions and royal judges would prove the Letter of Majesty could be hollowed out by procedure without ever being revoked.
historian_note: Wilson's reading is especially useful here: the Habsburg position was technically legalistic rather than simply lawless, but its political handling was dangerous. That is the central historical tradeoff for this card.

options.label: Confirm the strict line — uphold the closures, the arrests, the royal judges.
options.consequence: Catholic officials report that the new king will not retreat. The Bohemian Protestants carry the orders into their assemblies as evidence that the law itself is being turned against the charter by which they still profess obedience.

options.label: Suspend the disputed closures and call for an orderly clarification in law.
options.consequence: The petitioners can still tell their assemblies that procedure carries force. The Catholic allies hear hesitation from a prince whose whole reputation rests on restoring the rights they believe usurped.

options.label: Let Cardinal Klesl and the moderates seek a settlement, the royal claims reserved.
options.consequence: Envoys keep a channel open, and neither side need yet confess defeat. Ferdinand's harder allies see only delay; the radicals among the Defensors gain time to ready their answer.

title: Windows in Prague
briefing: For nine years an uneasy peace had held in Bohemia on the strength of a single document — the Letter of Majesty, which guaranteed the Protestant estates their churches, their schools, and their worship. In 1617 those same estates accepted Ferdinand, a Styrian archduke famous for stamping out Protestantism in his own duchy, as their next king; only two delegates voted no. Ferdinand confirmed their privileges and believed he was keeping them. Then royal officials closed one Protestant church and pulled another down, arrested the men who complained, and set royal judges over parish funds. To Count Thurn and the Defensors, the charter was being dismantled clause by clause.
situation: On 23 May 1618 Thurn led an armed assembly up the narrow stair of the Hradschin and threw two Catholic regents and their secretary from a high window. The act — at once called the Defenestration of Prague, after a Hussite revolt two centuries before — should have killed them; instead all three, astonishingly, survived the fall. The rebels insist they have struck not at the dynasty but at the 'evil advisers' who turned the king against his subjects; their cause, they say, is the Letter of Majesty itself. The first answer from Vienna will decide what this becomes: a riot to be punished, a lawsuit to be heard, or a war.
historian_note: The 1609 Letter of Majesty matters here because it turns Bohemian religious claims into a chartered estate-liberty problem: religion, schools, churches, defenders, and recorded royal protection all sit behind the rebels' language of privilege.

options.label: Treat the rising as a breach of the public peace — law, not the scaffold — and promise the chartered liberties will be reviewed, not revoked.
options.consequence: The legal line gives the cautious estates a reason to keep their loyalty; the Catholic hardliners hear in it the preserving of the very charter they had wished buried.

options.label: Brand the defenestrators traitors and their appeal to the Letter of Majesty a mask for revolt.
options.consequence: The Catholic allies applaud the plainness of it. The wavering estates hear that a recorded royal promise will not shelter them once obedience has failed — and begin to wonder whether they are safer in arms.

options.label: Offer to negotiate the disputed articles of the Letter of Majesty, if the rebels first reaffirm Habsburg kingship.
options.consequence: The moderates are given a bridge back to obedience — but a bridge that narrows how far any later victory might carry the Catholic restoration.

title: The Cardinal in the Way
briefing: At the centre of the emperor Matthias's government stood Cardinal Klesl, the architect of a policy of patience: hold the Protestants by negotiation, and preserve imperial authority by never forcing a confrontation. With Prague in open revolt, that patience now looked to Ferdinand and the hardline archdukes like paralysis. Klesl's letters still promised that Bohemia could be talked down; meanwhile the rebels seized offices, raised men, and emptied the treasury.
situation: Ferdinand's circle wanted a free hand, and Klesl stood in the way of it. The cardinal could still reach the moderate estates, and to remove him would breach every form — he was Matthias's minister, not Ferdinand's to dismiss. Yet every week of negotiation left the revolt in possession of the kingdom and the war chest unfilled.
historian_note: Backend note: Wilson treats Klesl's removal as a real inflection, but the peace alternative remains inferred and requires later source checking.

options.label: Keep Klesl at the table, and demand Prague disarm before any further grace.
options.consequence: The court keeps a channel to the moderates open — but the Catholic councillors complain that time and money are being handed to men already in arms.

options.label: Remove Klesl from power and prepare a harder answer.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand and Archduke Maximilian had the cardinal seized on 20 July 1618 and spirited to a fortress in the Tyrol, without Matthias's knowledge. The chancery now moves with fewer scruples and the war chest mends — but Prague sees that Vienna no longer means to bargain.

options.label: Set Klesl aside in public, but quietly use his contacts to keep one door open.
options.consequence: The hardliners hear that Ferdinand is no longer ruled by a cardinal's caution, while Prague receives just enough signal to keep talking.

title: Terms Carried Between Courts
briefing: Even after the rising, lines of negotiation still ran between Vienna and Prague — carried by Klesl's old agents, by doubtful nobles, and by men who insisted they fought for their privileges and not against the dynasty. Neither the Protestant directors nor the emperor's moderates had yet despaired of a settlement.
situation: But the terms on offer were narrower than Prague wanted and slower than the Catholic party would bear. A paper settlement was still possible — if either side would accept less than it had publicly sworn to win.
historian_note: Backend note: this is a Wilson-inferred alternate branch from Klesl's conciliatory role, not a claim that peace would certainly have followed.

options.label: Accept a narrow settlement: the directors disarm, the royal authority stands.
options.consequence: The moderates gain words to carry home — but neither the directors nor the Catholic party get the victory each promised its friends, and both begin to look past the table.

options.label: Let the talks collapse rather than concede the crown's disputed rights.
options.consequence: The language of negotiation is spent. Those who always said Vienna meant only delay now find the readier listeners, and both sides turn to their armies.

title: The Storm at Vienna
briefing: By the summer of 1619 the revolt had spilled out of Bohemia. Count Thurn crossed the Austrian frontier with ten thousand men and marched on Vienna itself, gambling that a blow at the Habsburg capital would bring the wavering Moravians and Austrians off the fence. Inside the city, Protestant nobles of Lower Austria pressed into Ferdinand's presence to demand guarantees for their religion before they would swear obedience.
situation: The palace waited on cavalry that might not arrive in time. Legend would say a Protestant deputy seized Ferdinand by the buttons, and that he knelt before a crucifix praying for deliverance — at the very moment Dampierre's horsemen clattered into the courtyard. To yield now, under armed pressure, would be heard in Prague as surrender; to refuse, with Thurn at the gates, might be heard as folly.
historian_note: Backend note: Wilson supports the actual pattern of firmness followed by selective reassurance; broader alternatives are inferred from the pressure field.

options.label: Stand firm until the loyal horse reaches the city.
options.consequence: In the event, Dampierre's arquebusiers dispersed the deputies, and Thurn — without siege guns and with no signal from his friends inside — retreated on 12 June. The danger passed, and the boldest petitioners were left exposed as conspirators.

options.label: Confirm individual nobles' privileges in return for their homage.
options.consequence: The moderates receive something they can accept without joining Prague. Corporate unity weakens — but the crown has admitted, in writing, that it must bargain with frightened estates.

options.label: Grant a broad corporate guarantee to quiet Lower Austria.
options.consequence: The immediate danger eases. But Prague learns that armed pressure can draw written security out of Ferdinand, and stores the lesson.

title: The Crown and the Electors
briefing: While Thurn besieged Vienna, the throne of the Holy Roman Empire fell vacant: Matthias was dead, and the seven electors gathered at Frankfurt to choose his successor. Ferdinand, as king of Bohemia, held an electoral vote himself — but the rebel estates argued that his Bohemian kingship was forfeit, that he had never been freely elected, and that they were entitled to choose another. Their reasoning drew on the Letter of Majesty, which had made religious liberty part of Bohemia's fundamental law.
situation: The two crowns now hung together. If Ferdinand could secure the imperial title, he would answer the rebels from the highest seat in Christendom; if the Bohemians could make their case first, they might depose him and bestow their crown elsewhere — and they were already turning to Frederick of the Palatinate. Everything turned on whether this was treated as a question of law, to be argued, or of authority, to be asserted.
historian_note: A 1619 Bohemian estates text frames Ferdinand's problem as legal, confessional, and dynastic, not merely military. The 1609 Letter of Majesty explains why the dispute could be presented as defense of recorded liberties rather than simple disobedience. The likely effects of each response still need direct review in Wilson and Asch.

options.label: Court the electors and make the imperial title the first answer to Prague.
options.consequence: The imperial crown steadies Ferdinand's hand and lifts him above the Bohemian estates. Their charter arguments still circulate — but now he answers them from a higher seat.

options.label: Denounce the estates' reasoning as rebellion dressed in the language of charter.
options.consequence: The crown refuses to let Prague define the law. The cautious estates hear that old liberties may be judged after obedience, not before it — and the militants hear a door closing.

options.label: Publish a legal rebuttal and promise a controlled review of the Letter's protections.
options.consequence: Ferdinand answers the estates on their own ground. The zealous allies dislike granting rebels the dignity of an argument, and the promised review may bind his later settlement.

title: Frankfurt's Oath
briefing: On 28 August 1619 the electors chose Ferdinand Holy Roman Emperor — unanimously, for even the Bohemian vote was cast in his favour, on the very day the rebels in Prague were declaring him deposed and electing Frederick in his place. The ceremony gave Ferdinand the regalia, the acclamation, and the coronation oath of the highest office in Christendom.
situation: But that oath cut both ways. The same imperial dignity that let Ferdinand answer Prague as a rebellion against the whole Empire also gave the electors and estates a written standard by which to measure him. He could present every act of force as the lawful defence of imperial order — or be seen to have bound his own hands before the war was even won.
historian_note: The English news pamphlet is useful because it places the coronation beside active crisis reporting and describes the public machinery of legitimacy: elector and ambassador roles, Golden Bull offices, regalia, acclamation, and oaths. It proves contemporary framing and ceremony, not the deeper causal weight of the coronation; that still needs direct comparison with modern scholarship.

options.label: Use Frankfurt as proof that Prague now defies the lawful emperor, not merely its king.
options.consequence: The crown raises Ferdinand's voice above the Bohemian estates and turns a dynastic quarrel into a matter of imperial law. It also makes every act of coercion sound like an imperial precedent that other princes will remember.

options.label: Publish the coronation as a promise of law, consultation, and protected privilege.
options.consequence: The moderate estates gain a language for loyalty without surrendering every fear. The Catholic allies hear the new emperor binding his own hands before the fight is won.

options.label: Keep the imperial ceremony apart from Bohemia, lest the revolt become an imperial test case.
options.consequence: Ferdinand blunts the sense that the new crown is aimed straight at Prague — but leaves his opponents more room to argue that the Bohemian dispute stands on its own separate law.

title: The Bavarian Bargain
briefing: The imperial title had not produced an army. Bohemia, Transylvania under Bethlen Gabor, and Frederick's supporters pressed on every side, and Ferdinand's own treasury was empty. The one prince who could put a disciplined Catholic army into the field at once was Maximilian of Bavaria, master of the Catholic League and patron of its veteran commander, Tilly.
situation: But Maximilian's help came on Maximilian's terms. By the Treaty of Munich he would march as the emperor's auxiliary — and be repaid in full, with part of Austria pledged as security and a tacit claim on the Palatinate's lands and electoral title should the war be won. Ferdinand called it taking the Bavarian devil to drive out the Bohemian Beelzebub. The alternative was to wait for an imperial army that did not exist while the rebellion hardened into a new order.
historian_note: Valeš's legal-history article reads the 1619 Munich Treaty as an emergency bargain: Maximilian receives direction of Catholic defense preparations, Ferdinand accepts compensation obligations, and Article II restricts separate negotiation, peace, or truces with Protestants without Bavarian knowledge and cooperation. The treaty text itself is still an acquisition target, while Ferdinand's 1619 election capitulation adds the constitutional pressure that war, burdens, alliances, and legitimacy must still look lawful.

options.label: Accept Maximilian's Munich terms — League command, full compensation, lands as security.
options.consequence: Bavarian columns under Tilly give the cause its teeth, and the revolt's days are numbered. But Maximilian now holds a claim on the command, the compensation, and any future peace — a creditor as much as an ally.

options.label: Seek a broader subscription of electors and Catholic estates first.
options.consequence: The dependence is spread more widely and wears a more constitutional face — but Maximilian's army is slower to move, and ready money stays scarce while the rebels gather strength.

options.label: Refuse the bonds of separate compensation and raise an imperial force instead.
options.consequence: Ferdinand keeps more of his freedom — and less of an army. The Bohemian and Transylvanian emergencies will not wait on a cleaner instrument.

memory_variants.briefing: Munich's hand was already strong, for the court had earlier embraced the Catholic League as the necessary answer to Protestant union. Maximilian and the League now appeared not as petitioners but as the instrument already chosen for the rescue — and the veteran Tilly with them.
memory_variants.situation: Bohemia, Transylvania, and Frederick's adherents still made a present problem of force. But the price by the Treaty of Munich was the sharper now: Bavarian command, full compensation, and a voice in the settlement followed from an earlier policy as much as from present necessity.

memory_variants.briefing: Because the leagues had earlier been suffered as lawful instruments of the public peace, Munich could offer its aid in the same guarded language. Maximilian and the Catholic League promised rescue while professing obedience — Tilly's veterans at their command.
memory_variants.situation: The offer was useful because it wore the face of law; it was dangerous because the army that saved Bohemia would carry, by the Treaty of Munich, its claims for command, compensation, and consultation.

memory_variants.briefing: The court's earlier condemnation of the leagues returned now as an awkwardness. Maximilian could still help — with Tilly and the Catholic League — but Vienna had to explain why a Catholic armed association was unlawful in principle yet indispensable in practice.
memory_variants.situation: Bohemia required force before any imperial levy could answer. To accept Bavarian aid by the Treaty of Munich, on these terms, was to make necessity stronger than the very law once invoked against faction.

title: Saxony and the Union
briefing: Ferdinand's deepest fear was that the revolt would fuse into a single Protestant cause. The one man who could prevent it was John George of Saxony — the senior Lutheran prince of the Empire, who despised the Calvinist Palatinate, distrusted Frederick's adventure, and valued imperial order above confessional solidarity. But he needed to be seen protecting Lutheran rights, not serving a Catholic crusade.
situation: Handled as a question of law and loyalty, Saxony might be brought to act against Prague — and John George had his price, the Lusatian lands he could occupy in the emperor's name. Handled as a holy war, he would stand aside, and the Protestant estates might close ranks behind Frederick. The framing of the appeal would decide which Saxony answered.
historian_note: Saxony is modeled as a legalist Protestant power, not as a simple confessional enemy. The election capitulation gives Ferdinand a direct vocabulary for reassurance: religious peace, Landfrieden, estate rights, and due process.

options.label: Promise Saxony that the religious peace and estate rights will be respected.
options.consequence: Saxon cooperation grows easier, and with it the chance to isolate Frederick. The Catholic hardliners mutter that the emperor is bargaining with heresy.

options.label: Demand Saxony prove its loyalty before any talk of assurances.
options.consequence: Ferdinand asserts his command — but Saxony hears obedience placed before the law the emperor swore to uphold, and grows colder.

options.label: Leave the matter to Bavaria and the Catholic allies; Saxony may follow or stand aside.
options.consequence: Catholic unity is cleaner without Lutheran partners — but the constitutional, legal language that might have split the Protestants from Frederick goes unused.

title: The Road to Prague
briefing: By autumn 1620 the allied armies had driven the revolt back toward its heart. Maximilian and the imperial forces stood in Bohemia, but the commanders disagreed: the cautious Bucquoy wanted to consolidate, while Tilly urged a swift march on Prague before winter closed the campaign and gave Frederick a reprieve.
situation: Ferdinand overruled his own general and placed him under Maximilian's command. A direct thrust at Prague might bring down the rebel crown in a single battle — or strand the army before a hard city in a bad season. The road led toward a chalk ridge just west of the capital, the White Mountain.
historian_note: Backend note: Wilson supports the actual direct march and political collapse; alternate campaign outcomes remain inferred.

options.label: Back Tilly: march directly on Prague and force a battle.
options.consequence: In the event, the army slipped round the rebel position and raced for the city; on 8 November 1620, at the White Mountain, it shattered the Confederate army in barely an hour. Frederick fled, and Bohemia lay open to whatever Ferdinand chose to make of victory.

options.label: Take Bucquoy's slower, surer approach through Moravia.
options.consequence: The campaign promises firmer ground and fewer winter hazards — but gives Prague more time to gather courage, coin, and allies, and leaves the rebel crown standing into another year.

options.label: Halt for winter and consolidate the allied positions.
options.consequence: The army is spared a perilous finish — but victory loses its terror, and the Confederates keep a court and a cause alive around Frederick through the cold months.

title: After White Mountain
briefing: White Mountain had been more than a victory; it was an annihilation. In barely an hour the Bohemian army had broken, Frederick had fled Prague with his court, and the kingdom that had defied the Habsburgs for two years lay open and undefended. Ferdinand now held something rare in the Empire: a rebellion entirely at his mercy.
situation: The question was what to make of such completeness. He could treat the revolt as treason and punish its leaders to terrify a generation; he could punish narrowly and keep law enough to part ringleaders from frightened followers; or he could offer broad pardon and bind Bohemia by gratitude rather than fear. Each road wrote a different future into the conquered kingdom.
historian_note: The card does not assume victory automatically produces stability. It asks what kind of victory Ferdinand makes.

options.label: Mark the leading rebels for exemplary punishment, and let the lesson travel.
options.consequence: The Habsburg grip tightens, and the warning carries far beyond Prague. But terror makes martyrs as readily as subjects, and frightened estates note that obedience offered no protection.

options.label: Punish the ringleaders, but keep law enough to part rebels from the mass of estates.
options.consequence: The settlement is severe yet legible, and gives the moderate estates less reason to panic. The zealous complain that mercy is wasted on traitors.

options.label: Offer broad amnesty to estates that swear renewed obedience.
options.consequence: Fear recedes and the kingdom quiets faster — but the Catholic allies, who fought for a reckoning, see a thorough restoration slipping from their hands.

title: The Blood Court
briefing: The tribunals in Prague had done their work, and the sentences lay on Ferdinand's desk: death for the leaders of the revolt. Even Slavata and Martinitz — the regents thrown from the window — counselled mercy, and the vice-chancellor urged the galleys instead of the axe. But to Ferdinand the revolt was treason, and treason had its price.
situation: He could make the punishment a public spectacle, teaching obedience by terror; he could commute most sentences and reserve death for a prominent few; or he could spare lives entirely and strike instead at names and lands through exile and confiscation. The Old Town Square waited on his answer.
historian_note: Backend note: Wilson explicitly calls the executions unnecessary and a mistake, making this a high-confidence alternate branch.

options.label: Sign the death warrants and let the executions be public.
options.consequence: In the event, twenty-seven men — three lords, seven knights, seventeen burghers — were beheaded or hanged in the Old Town Square on 21 June 1621; twelve heads and the rector's tongue were nailed over the gates, where they stayed until 1631. Wilson calls it unnecessary and a mistake: it made the dead into martyrs, and Prague's sympathy turned back toward the rebels.

options.label: Commute most sentences; reserve death for the most prominent few.
options.consequence: Treason is still marked, but Prague sees that obedience need not end on the scaffold for every condemned man — and the court keeps a measure of mercy it can spend later.

options.label: Spare lives; punish through humiliation, exile, and confiscation instead.
options.consequence: Names and lands are struck while lives are spared. The hardliners call it weakness — but no household is handed a martyr to mourn.

title: Lands for Loyalty
briefing: Victory had to be paid for. Ferdinand owed his soldiers, his Bavarian and Spanish allies, and the loyal nobles who had stood by him — and the defeated rebels owned half of Bohemia. Their estates could be confiscated to fund the settlement, reward friends, and remake the kingdom's ruling class in Catholic and loyal hands.
situation: But confiscation on a grand scale would tell every estate in the Empire that defeat meant not merely punishment but extinction — the loss of land, status, and posterity. The crown could seize boldly and transform Bohemia at a stroke, confiscate with restraint and a public record, or commute seizures to fines and oaths and leave the defeated something to lose.
historian_note: Confiscation is modeled as fiscal policy, social transformation, and a fear signal at once.

options.label: Confiscate on a grand scale to reward the loyal and fund the war.
options.consequence: In the event, nearly half the land in Bohemia changed hands, building a new aristocracy of Catholic loyalists, foreigners, and war profiteers — Wallenstein chief among them. Money and loyalty flow through the seized estates; so does the terror of total defeat.

options.label: Confiscate selectively, with a public legal record of each case.
options.consequence: The settlement pays more slowly, but wears less the look of appetite crowned. Fewer neutral estates are pushed to conclude that loyalty offers no safety either.

options.label: Commute many seizures to fines and renewed oaths.
options.consequence: Less is gathered and less transformed — but more of the defeated are left with property, and so with a stake in not rebelling again.

title: The Spanish Road
briefing: The war had reached the Rhine, and there it touched a Spanish nerve. Frederick's Palatine homeland straddled the Spanish Road — the corridor by which Spain marched men and silver from Italy to its war against the Dutch. With the Dutch truce expiring in 1621, Madrid had every reason to hold the Rhenish Palatinate, and Spinola's army had already occupied it.
situation: Spanish help against Frederick was real and close at hand — but it came tangled in Spain's own war, and it made the imperial quarrel look like a Habsburg family enterprise spanning Europe. Ferdinand could embrace the coordination openly, take the help quietly while keeping imperial policy separate, or hold Spain at arm's length and insist the matter was purely German.
historian_note: The card abstracts Spanish Habsburg strategic interest without pretending the Empire and Spain had identical goals. Ferdinand's capitulation makes foreign alliances and foreign troops a constitutional sensitivity, not merely a diplomatic preference.

options.label: Coordinate openly with Spain along the Rhine and in the Palatinate.
options.consequence: Dynastic Habsburg power gathers on a continental scale, and Frederick is squeezed from two sides. So do the fears of every state — Dutch, French, English — that watches the Rhine and sees Madrid and Vienna acting as one.

options.label: Take Spanish help quietly, but keep imperial policy visibly separate.
options.consequence: Ferdinand gains soldiers without making the Empire look like Madrid's instrument — a harder line to walk, and one that fully satisfies neither the Spanish nor the purists at court.

options.label: Hold Spain at arm's length; frame the war as a purely imperial matter.
options.consequence: The legal story stays clean and German — but the practical resources are thinner, and the Palatinate is the harder to subdue without Spanish arms.

title: Who Pays the League?
briefing: The victories had not stopped the bills. The Catholic League's army — the instrument that won White Mountain — had to be paid, and Maximilian expected the emperor to find the money. Imperial officers, creditors, and the occupied territories all pressed on the same exhausted treasury.
situation: Armies did not live on legitimacy. Ferdinand could squeeze the occupied and even loyal lands harder through war contributions, borrow against future confiscations and dynastic credit, or trim the war's aims until his finances could bear them. Each choice decided who paid for victory, and how much resentment came with the bill.
historian_note: This card makes finance a central political constraint rather than a background number.

options.label: Levy heavier war contributions on occupied and loyal lands alike.
options.consequence: The army stays fed, and the system of making war pay for itself takes root. The countryside learns that loyalty buys no immunity from the soldiers' demands.

options.label: Borrow against future confiscations and dynastic credit.
options.consequence: Some immediate suffering is spared — but the crown's future narrows around its debts, and the men who lend expect repayment in land, office, or influence.

options.label: Trim the war's aims until finance can catch up with ambition.
options.consequence: The war draws breath and the treasury recovers — but the allies who fought for a reckoning ask why they are made to stop short of it.

title: The Ban of Frederick
briefing: Frederick had fled, but his claim had not. As an elector of the Empire he could still gather money, men, and sympathy across Protestant Europe. Ferdinand could end that by placing him under the imperial ban — the Empire's highest sanction, making him an outlaw whom every subject was bound to deny aid. But to outlaw an elector was no ordinary act of discipline.
situation: The ban would give the victory the force of law and brand Frederick a rebel beyond the pale. Yet to impose it on an elector without the full Diet's hearing would teach every prince in the Empire that their rights, too, might be swept away by imperial decree. Ferdinand could issue the ban in its widest form, offer Frederick a conditional pardon, or proclaim the ban while reassuring the neutral princes that it touched one man alone.
historian_note: This card is grounded in Ferdinand's 22 January 1621 imperial-ban declaration, read against the 1619 capitulation's due-process promise. The decree says Frederick had incurred the Landfrieden penalties ipso facto, yet Ferdinand still issues a confirming declaration; that is exactly where legal force and process anxiety meet. The documents prove Ferdinand's legal framing and constitutional constraint, not by themselves how every estate interpreted the ban.

options.label: Place Frederick under the full imperial ban.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand outlawed Frederick in January 1621 with only a hand-picked few electors consulted, not the full Diet. The victory gained teeth in law — but even Catholic princes took alarm, for if an elector could be banned by fiat, no estate's rights were safe from the emperor's pen.

options.label: Offer Frederick pardon if he renounces Bohemia and disarms.
options.consequence: The moderates see an exit from the crisis; the Catholic allies see a rebel king handed one more door, and wonder whether victory will ever be used.

options.label: Outlaw Frederick, but reassure the neutral princes that it touches him alone.
options.consequence: The decree isolates one man instead of threatening every estate — but such restraint needs princes willing to trust the emperor's word about where the line stops.

title: The Paladins Remain in the Field
briefing: Heidelberg and Mannheim had fallen, yet the Palatine cause would not die. Two freebooting generals kept it alive: Ernst von Mansfeld, the mercenary who lived off the land, and Christian of Brunswick, the 'mad Halberstadter' who coined plundered church silver under the motto 'God's friend, priests' enemy.' English and Spanish envoys, meanwhile, hunted for terms each could call a peace.
situation: Ferdinand could punish Frederick to the end, bargain over a conditional restoration, or split the lesser Palatine supporters from the elector's ruin. But every course brushed against Maximilian, who had been promised the Palatinate's lands and electoral title as the price of his army — and who would read any leniency to Frederick as a theft from himself.
historian_note: Backend note: replaces the duplicate 1622 Frederick-ban card with Wilson's Regensburg and Palatine settlement problem.

options.label: Offer conditional restoration if Frederick renounces Bohemia and his armies disband.
options.consequence: The Palatine grievance is given a road back into law — but Maximilian hears that victory may not bring him the full price promised at Munich, and grows wary.

options.label: Keep the ban in force and pursue a settlement by arms.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand pressed on militarily and kept Frederick outlawed. No prince mistook the victory for weakness — but the Palatine name stayed alive in exile, a ready grievance for every foreign power that wanted one.

options.label: Separate Frederick's punishment from amnesty for his lesser supporters.
options.consequence: The elector stays marked while lesser men are offered a way home. The exile network loses some breadth — without satisfying Frederick's closest allies, who fight on.

options.label: Use Spanish and Bavarian pressure to force a settlement on Habsburg terms.
options.consequence: Allied force drives the settlement forward — but the Empire sees that Palatine law now moves in the shadow of Madrid and Munich, not Vienna.

title: Maximilian's Price
briefing: The bill from Munich now fell due. Maximilian had saved Ferdinand's cause, and the secret price had always been Frederick's electoral dignity — the vote that made the Palatinate one of the seven powers entitled to choose the emperor. To hand it to Bavaria would reward loyalty and crown the Catholic victory; it would also remake the electoral college by imperial will.
situation: The electors guarded their number jealously, and Protestant Saxony and Brandenburg would read the transfer as a warning: that an emergency bargain could permanently alter the constitution. Ferdinand could fulfil the promise outright, delay it while compensating Bavaria with lands and revenues, or punish Frederick yet preserve the electoral balance for now — and risk turning a disappointed Maximilian into a dangerous one.
historian_note: Valeš connects the 1623 settlement to an earlier secret oral promise attached to the 1619 Munich Treaty: Ferdinand offered Maximilian the Palatine electoral dignity and conquered Palatine territories, while knowing the promise exceeded his legal competence and would alarm German princes. The transfer option follows the historical direction; alternatives are plausible game abstractions, not asserted certainties.

options.label: Fulfil the promise and transfer the electoral title to Maximilian.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand transferred the dignity to Bavaria at Regensburg in 1623 — at first only for Maximilian's lifetime, a fig-leaf that fooled no one. Bavaria is rewarded and the Catholic victory crowned; but the electors have learned that a bargain struck in emergency can become a permanent fact of the constitution.

options.label: Delay the dignity, compensating Bavaria with lands and revenues instead.
options.consequence: The constitutional shock is softened — but Maximilian's patience becomes another debt, and one that gathers interest.

options.label: Punish Frederick, but keep the electoral balance untouched for now.
options.consequence: The electors are reassured by the restraint; Bavaria is not. A disappointed ally is an armed ally still.
options.unavailable_text: Bavarian claims now bind the settlement too tightly for a balance policy to be credible.

memory_variants.title: Maximilian's Claim
memory_variants.briefing: Regensburg had not ended Bavaria's claim. Maximilian's soldiers and credit had recovered the emperor's position, and the promise of the Treaty of Munich still hung over every Palatine compromise — Frederick's electoral dignity its unpaid price.
memory_variants.situation: A softer Palatine settlement left Ferdinand a sharper danger: if Frederick were not wholly stripped, Maximilian must still be satisfied without making the electoral college look a thing the emperor could give and take at will.

pressure_variants.briefing: The memorials from Munich no longer read as requests. They read as accounts due. Maximilian's service in Bohemia, the League's expense, and the unsettled Palatine title are now presented together.
pressure_variants.situation: The electors hear that the emperor must reward useful loyalty, but several courts warn that an electoral title cannot be moved without wounding the balance of the Empire.

title: A Victory That Will Not End
briefing: By 1623 Ferdinand had won. Bohemia was crushed, Frederick outlawed and stripped, the Palatinate occupied, the electoral title passed to Bavaria. And yet the Empire would not settle. The victory had bred its own enemies: ruined exiles, frightened Protestant princes, unpaid soldiers, rewarded allies who wanted more, and foreign powers newly alarmed by Habsburg success.
situation: Ferdinand stood at a crossroads few conquerors reach. He could try to turn victory back into law — calling a formal settlement to fix obedience and reassure the moderates — or press his advantage until no prince dared doubt imperial power, or bank the winnings, demobilize, and repair his exhausted finances. The first was slow, the second combustible, the third resented by the men who had profited from the war.
historian_note: This closing MVP card asks whether the player has made consolidation or escalation more likely.

options.label: Call a formal imperial settlement to lock in obedience and reassure moderates.
options.consequence: Ferdinand tries to convert victory into law — slower than command, but far less apt to catch fire. The hardliners grumble that strength is being given away at the table.

options.label: Press the advantage until no prince doubts imperial reach.
options.consequence: From Vienna the authority looks magnificent. From the Protestant courts it looks like a forecast — and abroad, like a reason to act before it is too late.

options.label: Demobilize what can be spared and spend on fiscal repair.
options.consequence: The war machine cools and the treasury mends — but the allies and officers who profited from its motion resist the stillness, and a half-paid army is its own danger.

title: Lower Saxony Will Not Stay Quiet
briefing: The war had reached the northern edge of the Empire. The Lower Saxon Circle — the league of north German territories that organized their own defence — grew alarmed as Catholic and imperial armies pressed toward the Baltic and its rich secularized bishoprics. At its head sat a formidable outsider: Christian IV of Denmark, who as Duke of Holstein was himself a prince of the circle, and who eyed those bishoprics for his own sons.
situation: The circle claimed only neutrality and self-defence. But to let an imperial circle decide for itself when imperial law applied was to concede a dangerous principle — and behind its assemblies stood Danish gold, English subsidies, and an army. Accept the neutrality unconditionally, and the north slips beyond the emperor's reach; refuse it, and Christian enters the war not as a distant king but as the armed protector of a threatened frontier.
historian_note: Wilson frames the Danish-Lower Saxon phase around neutrality, bishoprics, circle politics, and imperial authority.

options.label: Refuse a neutrality that merely shelters the Danish cause.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand pressed the issue, and in 1625 Christian IV took the field as the Lower Saxon Circle's elected colonel. Imperial firmness was heard in the north as a threat — and Denmark heard it as an invitation to lead the Protestant war.

options.label: Recognize a temporary circle neutrality, subject to imperial review.
options.consequence: The north buys a season's quiet — but Catholic petitioners ask whether imperial law now waits upon every circle's convenience, and the precedent sits uneasily.

options.label: Let the League's armies compel the wavering territories.
options.consequence: The language of law arrives with soldiers behind it. The warning is unmistakable — and so is the risk that armed pressure is exactly what tips the circle into Christian's arms.

title: A Field Army of Ferdinand's Own
briefing: Every victory so far had been won with another prince's army. Bavaria and the Catholic League had crushed Bohemia and the Palatinate — and Maximilian never let Ferdinand forget who held the sword. Then a Bohemian magnate made the emperor an extraordinary offer. Albrecht von Wallenstein, grown vastly rich on confiscated rebel estates, proposed to raise a great imperial army at his own credit and the country's expense.
situation: Wallenstein's secret was the contribution system: his colonels would feed, clothe, and pay their men by levying the lands they occupied, sparing the empty imperial treasury almost entirely. For the first time Ferdinand could have an army that answered to him and not to Munich. But such an army's purse lay in the territories it ravaged, and its officers looked upward not to the emperor but to Wallenstein.
historian_note: Wilson treats Wallenstein's system as both capacity solution and autonomous military-fiscal network.

pressure_variants.briefing: The treasury figures arrive in a poor hand and worse news. Arrears, pledges, and ally claims leave little room for an ordinary imperial army.

options.label: Accept Wallenstein's contribution army.
options.consequence: In the event, Wallenstein began recruiting in June 1625 and within months commanded a host larger than the League's — funded by squeezing the occupied lands. Ferdinand gained an army of his own; the country gained a machine that made war feed war, and a servant whose power would soon rival his master's.

options.label: Authorize a smaller army under tighter warrants.
options.consequence: The court keeps the commander on a shorter leash — and receives a smaller, slower instrument that leans it back toward Bavaria for the heavy work.

options.label: Rely on the League and Spain rather than build a new system.
options.consequence: Ferdinand avoids one dangerous servant by leaning harder on another. Maximilian's value rises again, and with it his price.

title: Frederick Nearly Bends
briefing: By 1627 the Danish war was going Ferdinand's way, and the exiled Frederick — landless, outlawed, his cause fading — let it be known he might yield at last. He would renounce Bohemia, accept Maximilian's hold on the Palatinate for life, and submit to the emperor, if only by proxy. After nine years, a negotiated end to the Palatine grievance was within reach.
situation: The sticking point was not whether Frederick would lose, but how visibly. A submission in person would humble him before all Europe and satisfy the Catholic party; a submission by proxy would spare him the humiliation and close the wound faster. Ferdinand could demand the full ceremony of defeat — or take the substance and let the form go.
historian_note: Wilson notes that agreement was close, but Ferdinand's demand for personal submission helped close the opening.

options.label: Require Frederick's submission in person to imperial authority.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand and his allies held out for the full humiliation, and the settlement slipped away on the question of form. The Palatine grievance stayed open — a standing invitation to every foreign power that wished the emperor ill.

options.label: Accept submission by proxy and secure the renunciations.
options.consequence: A humiliating journey is spared and the wound nearly closes — but Bavaria asks what certainty remains when rebellion can be settled by parchment, and the Catholic zealots feel cheated of their reckoning.

options.label: Trade a limited restoration for security and reparations.
options.consequence: The Palatine cause is split from the mercenary war — but every clause must pass through Bavarian suspicion, and Maximilian guards his prize.

title: Mandates in the Hereditary Lands
briefing: In the Habsburg hereditary lands — Bohemia, Moravia, Austria — victory was being made permanent in the only way Ferdinand wholly trusted: by faith. Pastors were expelled, churches inspected, offices closed to Protestants, and noble houses pressed to convert or sell up and leave. The Styrian method Ferdinand had perfected as an archduke was now the policy of an emperor at the height of his power.
situation: His Catholic loyalists pressed him to make the victory visible everywhere at once — in worship, schooling, marriage, office, and landholding. Others warned that sudden, total uniformity would drive property, skilled labour, and undying hatred abroad with the exiles. The pace of restoration was itself a decision.
historian_note: This card previews later overreach dynamics without jumping ahead to the Edict of Restitution.

options.label: Press a visible Catholic restoration across the recovered lands.
options.consequence: Catholic confidence surges and the hereditary lands are remade within a generation. But Protestant alarm learns to organize, and thousands carry their skills, their capital, and their grievance into exile.

options.label: Sequence the restoration slowly, after oaths and fiscal order.
options.consequence: The settlement advances on firmer ground — but not fast enough for the most zealous allies, who suspect every delay of weakness.

options.label: Suspend the major measures to calm Lutheran and city opinion.
options.consequence: The moderates breathe easier and the towns stay productive — but the Catholic allies wonder aloud what the victory was even for.

title: Mecklenburg as Payment
briefing: Wallenstein had made the emperor an army and now expected to be paid — not in arrears the treasury could not meet, but in land and title worthy of a victorious general. The dukes of Mecklenburg, who had backed the Danish invasion, lay under imperial displeasure and could be deposed. Their duchy would more than settle the account.
situation: To pay a servant with a prince's lands was easier than finding the money. But it would also tell every old house in the Empire that victory could move them out and set new men in — and would raise a Bohemian parvenu to the rank of imperial prince, a peer of families that had ruled for centuries.
historian_note: Wilson presents Wallenstein's elevation in Mecklenburg as a key overreach signal.

options.label: Grant Mecklenburg to Wallenstein, dukedom and all.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand made his general Duke of Mecklenburg in 1628, deposing its ancient line. The army's maker is paid in princely coin — but the whole Empire studies the precedent in fear, and the old princes begin to see in Wallenstein a threat to them all.

options.label: Grant the administration without a hereditary title.
options.consequence: Wallenstein receives the substance without the full shock of a ducal transfer. The distinction satisfies few — but alarms slightly fewer.

options.label: Find cash and movable confiscations instead.
options.consequence: The old dynastic order is spared a warning — but the treasury groans, and an unpaid general is a more dangerous creditor than a rewarded one.
options.unavailable_text: The treasury cannot credibly satisfy Wallenstein's arrears without using land, offices, or future contributions.

title: Peace at Lubeck
briefing: Christian IV had lost his war. Tilly and Wallenstein had beaten the Danes out of Germany and driven them back onto their islands, and the imperial armies stood triumphant on the Baltic shore. Now the king sued for terms, and Ferdinand had to decide what victory over a foreign crown was worth.
situation: A harsh peace — stripping Denmark, demanding compensation — would please the allies who hungered for spoils, but might keep Christian in the field when Sweden was already stirring behind him. A lenient peace would remove one enemy cleanly, at the cost of looking like weakness to friends who had bled for more. Wallenstein himself, with an eye on Sweden, urged moderation as terms took shape at Lübeck.
historian_note: Wilson emphasizes the generosity and strategic logic of Lubeck, especially the wish to remove Denmark.

options.label: Restore Denmark's lands if Christian abandons the north German cause.
options.consequence: In the event, the Peace of Lübeck (1629) let Christian keep his duchies in return for quitting the Empire's wars. Denmark left the field — but the north German Protestants he abandoned learned what an imperial peace cost them, and Sweden noted how far the emperor's reach now ran along the Baltic.

options.label: Demand compensation and harder guarantees from Denmark.
options.consequence: The war party applauds a sterner peace — but Christian hesitates to sign, and every month he lingers improves the Swedish king's calculations.

options.label: Use Lübeck to open a wider imperial settlement.
options.consequence: The hardliners protest that victory is being spent too cheaply — but the moderates glimpse, for the first time in years, a door toward a general peace.
options.unavailable_text: Too much alarm has gathered for a general settlement to be credible without first quieting Protestant security fears.

title: The Edict of Restitution
briefing: At the summit of his power, Ferdinand reached for a final settlement of the religious question that had started it all. His jurists held that the Peace of Augsburg, rightly read, entitled the Church to recover every ecclesiastical land the Protestants had taken since 1552 — two archbishoprics, a dozen bishoprics, scores of monasteries. What two generations of negotiation had left ambiguous, an emperor with an army could now simply declare.
situation: Issued as an edict rather than agreed in the Diet, and enforced by imperial commissioners, the Edict of Restitution would be the greatest Catholic gain of the war. It would also tell every Protestant prince — and not a few Catholic ones — that the emperor could rewrite the constitution by his own pen. The very completeness that made it possible was what made it dangerous.
historian_note: This card is grounded in Ferdinand's Edict of Restitution. The source gives the official legal-confessional case; the wider causal consequences still need direct review in modern scholarship.

options.label: Issue the Edict and send commissioners to enforce restitution.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand issued the Edict of Restitution on 6 March 1629. Catholic restoration gained the force of imperial command — and the Protestant estates heard the religious settlement being rewritten from Vienna by decree. It did more than any battle to drive them, in time, into Swedish arms.

options.label: Seek an elector- or Diet-backed interpretation before enforcing.
options.consequence: The law stays more shared and less explosive — but restoration slows, and the Catholic allies see victory losing its nerve at the decisive moment.

options.label: Enforce only the clearest cases of restitution for now.
options.consequence: The Edict has teeth but not yet jaws. Every party presses Ferdinand to say what comes next, and the uncertainty satisfies no one.

options.label: Hold the restitution claims back as material for a wider peace.
options.consequence: The Empire might yet breathe — but the most committed Catholic restorers will long remember what was left on the table when it could have been taken.
options.unavailable_text: Trust has fallen too low, or foreign danger has risen too far, for restitution to buy peace by bargain alone.

memory_variants.briefing: The lenient Peace of Lübeck had removed Denmark without opening a general settlement, and the Catholic petitioners now pressed that victory and peace together should let the old church claims be made good at last.
memory_variants.situation: A decree could satisfy them — but the same paper, the Edict of Restitution, might tell the Lutheran princes that moderation toward Denmark had been only the prelude to enforcement at home.

memory_variants.briefing: The mandates in the hereditary lands had already made the Catholic restoration visible in churches, schools, and offices. Now the same question arrived in imperial form, resting on the disputed reach of the Peace of Augsburg.
memory_variants.situation: To issue the Edict of Restitution was to carry the hereditary method into the whole Empire; to delay was to disappoint those who believed victory had already proved the method lawful.

memory_variants.briefing: The earlier willingness to settle the Palatine matter by proxy had kept a language of compromise alive. The restitution petitions, grounded on the Peace of Augsburg, now tested whether that restraint could survive a Catholic victory.
memory_variants.situation: A broad Edict of Restitution would reverse the tone of compromise at a stroke. A narrower reading might keep the wavering Lutheran estates from treating every imperial paper as a threat.

title: Regensburg: The Price of Consent
briefing: In 1630 Ferdinand summoned the electors to Regensburg at the summit of his power, wanting two things: their consent to elect his son King of the Romans, securing the succession, and their help against his enemies. He arrived to find the mood transformed. The Edict, the contributions, Mecklenburg, and above all Wallenstein's looming army had convinced even Catholic electors that the emperor had grown too strong.
situation: The electors would consider nothing until Ferdinand sacrificed his generalissimo. To dismiss Wallenstein would buy their goodwill and quiet the constitutional alarm — but it would also disarm the emperor at the very moment a new danger landed: for as the congress sat, Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden came ashore in Pomerania. Several advisers feared the slighted general might turn his army on Vienna itself.
historian_note: Wilson treats Regensburg as collective imperial politics checking Ferdinand's overreach.

options.label: Dismiss Wallenstein to recover the electors' consent.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand sacrificed his general in 1630 — and the all-powerful generalissimo went quietly to his estates. The electors got their sacrifice; but the emperor had disarmed himself just as Gustavus Adolphus invaded, and within a year the Swede would overrun half of Germany.

options.label: Keep Wallenstein, with his powers reduced.
options.consequence: The army stays in being, but the electors' consent thins, and the congress turns from a settlement into a warning. Ferdinand keeps his sword and loses the goodwill he came to win.

options.label: Offer to reform the army in exchange for his son's election.
options.consequence: The bargain guards the dynasty more than the field army — and the electors, jealous of their last great leverage, are slow to part with the succession for so little.

title: The Door Stands Open
briefing: Gustavus Adolphus had landed, and the Protestant estates were no longer asking merely for delay. With the Edict being enforced by imperial commissioners and a Swedish army on German soil, Saxony and the Lutheran princes met at Leipzig and spoke openly of armed self-defence — a third force, neither imperial nor Swedish, to protect their rights.
situation: The Leipzig assembly was not yet rebellion, but it was the door to it. If Ferdinand offered no public settlement — above all on the Edict — the wavering middle might cease to be middle and fall in with Sweden. If he conceded too much, his Catholic allies would ask what the years of victory and the Edict had been for. The choice was whether to command the Lutherans or to bargain with them.
historian_note: Wilson says Ferdinand's refusal of the Leipzig off-ramp compounded the Edict error and helped drive Saxony toward Sweden.

options.label: Reject the Leipzig convention and order the Lutherans to disarm.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand refused to bend, and Saxon neutrality broke under the weight of command. Driven to choose, John George allied with Gustavus — and that autumn their joined armies destroyed Tilly's at Breitenfeld, the first great Protestant victory of the war.

options.label: Suspend the Edict and accept Saxon mediation.
options.consequence: The Catholic party murmurs at the retreat — but the Lutheran elector stays within reach, and the third force may yet be kept from Sweden's arms.

options.label: Offer private concessions while refusing any public bloc.
options.consequence: Ferdinand tries to buy trust without confessing necessity. Whether it works depends entirely on how much trust is left — and after the Edict, there is not much.

memory_variants.briefing: The Edict now travelled ahead of every imperial envoy, and Gustavus Adolphus had landed besides. Saxony and the Protestant estates no longer asked merely for delay; they asked whether obedience could live beside the security only an army could give.
memory_variants.situation: Driven by the Edict, the Leipzig assembly leaned toward armed self-defence. Offer no public settlement and the middle falls to Sweden; concede too much and the Catholic allies ask what the Edict was for.

memory_variants.briefing: Because restitution had been treated as a matter for bargaining rather than command alone, the Saxon envoys still had language enough to ask for public terms before they chose Gustavus Adolphus and his arms.
memory_variants.situation: Sweden was on German soil, but the Lutheran middle had not yet lost every reason to deal with the emperor — if the Edict could be seen to bend.

title: Saxony Crosses the Line
briefing: It had come to the thing Ferdinand most feared. John George of Saxony — the cautious Lutheran who had once invaded Lusatia for the emperor — would no longer trust a suspension of the Edict given by private word. The decree still stood in public; Leipzig had been rebuffed; and a Swedish army now offered the security that imperial law no longer seemed to provide.
situation: John George was no natural rebel; his defection showed something worse for Ferdinand — that even a loyal Lutheran elector could be driven from guarded obedience into armed alliance with a foreign king, once the terms of obedience looked unsafe. The emperor could treat the break as rebellion and prepare for a wider war, or send public terms at last to pull Saxony back before the bond with Sweden hardened.
historian_note: Wilson links Ferdinand's refusal of the Leipzig off-ramp to Saxony's movement toward Sweden after the Edict of Restitution had already frightened Lutheran moderates.

options.label: Treat the Saxon alignment as rebellion and prepare for a wider imperial war.
options.consequence: In the event, Saxony joined Sweden, and at Breitenfeld in September 1631 their armies shattered Tilly's. The court kept the language of command — but now an elector's obedience, and half of Germany, would have to be won back by the sword.

options.label: Send public suspension terms to part Saxony from Sweden.
options.consequence: Envoys carry a late offer that might loosen the Saxon bond — but cannot erase the proof that it took armed pressure to wring the paper from Vienna.

title: Gollersdorf
briefing: Breitenfeld had been a catastrophe. Tilly was beaten and soon dead, the Swedes had overrun the south, and Bavaria itself was invaded. The army Ferdinand had dismissed to please the electors was precisely what he now needed — and only one man could rebuild it at speed. The disgraced Wallenstein received the emperor's envoys again.
situation: But Wallenstein would not return as a servant to be corrected at every ally's complaint. The price of his recall was near-sovereign authority over the army — the powers he would extract at Gollersdorf. Without him, Ferdinand was left to Bavaria and a patchwork of scattered commands against the finest soldier in Europe.
historian_note: Wilson presents Wallenstein's recall as necessity joined to broad delegation.

options.label: Recall Wallenstein with the broad powers of Gollersdorf.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand granted his general almost unlimited authority, and Wallenstein rebuilt an imperial army within months. The crown got its instrument back — and handed it to a man whose loyalty it could no longer command, only hope for.

options.label: Recall him under written limits.
options.consequence: The court asks for a safer miracle. Wallenstein weighs whether a command hedged with conditions is worth the taking — and the army it might raise is slower and smaller.

options.label: Build a coalition command without him.
options.consequence: The old dependence on Bavaria returns, under worse circumstances. Maximilian is necessary once more — and the Swede does not wait.

title: The General Makes His Own Peace
briefing: Gustavus Adolphus had fallen at Lützen, and the Swedish thunderbolt was spent — yet the war did not end, because the man who could end it now seemed to be playing his own game. Through 1633 Wallenstein held his great army nearly idle, opened secret talks with the Swedes, the Saxons, and the exiles, and let no one be sure whether he sought peace for the emperor or for himself.
situation: His letters and his silences could be read two ways. To tolerate his diplomacy might split the enemy coalition; to supervise it might provoke him; to prepare a replacement might turn suspicion into open rupture. And behind every reading lay the question no one in Vienna could answer with certainty: where did the loyalty of the army's officers finally lie?
historian_note: Wilson treats Wallenstein's opaque diplomacy as a real source of mistrust even if outright treason remains difficult to prove cleanly.

options.label: Quietly build Spanish and Bavarian alternatives to Wallenstein.
options.consequence: In the event, Ferdinand began preparing to do without his general — and Wallenstein, reading the plan as an accusation, drew closer to his secret contacts. Trust had become a military plan; the breach was now only a matter of time.

options.label: Authorize his peace soundings under an explicit warrant.
options.consequence: Ferdinand turns a danger into an instrument — but every ally dreads what the instrument might sign, and the leash is only as strong as the general's word.

options.label: Confront him and renegotiate his powers face to face.
options.consequence: The wound is opened before the army has chosen its side — a gamble on whether the officers serve the emperor or the man who pays them.

title: Dead or Alive
briefing: By early 1634 Vienna was convinced its generalissimo meant treason. Wallenstein had bound his colonels to himself by oath, opened unmistakable contacts with the enemy, and ignored imperial orders. Patents were being drawn to release the officers from their obedience — but they would be lawful only if the army first ceased to be his.
situation: An arrest meant a trial, and a trial meant delay and exposure while the army wavered. A removal by force would settle the matter at a stroke and recover the command — but the chancery would inherit the stain of a murder done in the emperor's name. Either way, the question was whether the officers would obey Vienna or Wallenstein when the moment came.
historian_note: Wilson describes Ferdinand's patents and the political burial after Eger.

options.label: Release the officers and authorize his removal, dead or alive.
options.consequence: In the event, Wallenstein was cut down with his closest officers at Eger on 25 February 1634. The army returned at once to obedience — but the manner of it, an assassination by imperial warrant, was a stain the crown would carry, and a warning every great servant would remember.

options.label: Arrest him for trial before imperial authority.
options.consequence: The lawful road is cleaner and far slower — and every day of it gives the army time to ask whom it truly serves.

options.label: Reconcile with him and narrow his command.
options.consequence: The crisis is postponed inside a smaller circle — but Bavaria and Spain do not mistake postponement for safety, and the general's grievance only deepens.

title: The Peace of Prague
briefing: The victory at Nördlingen in 1634 changed everything. With the main Swedish army broken and his own son the hero of the hour, Ferdinand could at last negotiate from strength. He reached for a general peace with the German estates: he would suspend the hated Edict, draw Saxony and the Lutherans back to obedience, and unite all their armies under imperial command to drive the foreigners out.
situation: The opportunity was real, and the danger lay in the fine print. A broad amnesty would heal the Empire but disappoint the men who had fought for a reckoning; a narrow one would reward loyalists but leave the excluded — princes, exiles, and armies — with nothing to lose and France and Sweden glad to employ them. Every name left outside the pardon was a future enemy.
historian_note: Wilson calls Prague a broad settlement undermined by exclusions.

options.label: Make the elector's peace and leave the hard cases excluded.
options.consequence: In the event, Saxony, Brandenburg, and most Lutheran estates accepted Ferdinand's terms on 30 May 1635, and the war lost its confessional edge. But Ferdinand's exclusion of certain princes and exiles from the amnesty — Wilson calls it a grave error — kept a dissatisfied minority in arms and gave France and Sweden the clients they needed to fight on for thirteen more years.

options.label: Broaden the amnesty while protecting the core loyalist rewards.
options.consequence: The settlement cuts deeper into the enemy's German support — but the loyal beneficiaries ask which of their promised rewards will now be clawed back to buy off rebels.
options.unavailable_text: Too much trust has been spent for a broad amnesty to command belief.

options.label: Use Nördlingen to demand a harder Catholic settlement.
options.consequence: Victory is spent like a confession of strength. The peace party thins, the excluded multiply, and the foreign crowns gain still more clients for the war that will not end.

memory_variants.briefing: With Wallenstein cut down at Eger and the Swedes broken at Nördlingen, the Saxon articles came within reach. The court could speak again of imperial order — though officers and princes remembered how that order had been recovered.
memory_variants.situation: The Edict could be suspended, the armies joined under the emperor, the Lutheran estates brought home. The danger, as ever, lay in the names left outside the pardon, ready for France or Sweden.

memory_variants.briefing: Because restitution had already been treated as negotiable peace business, the Saxon articles after Nördlingen arrived less as a surrender than as a form the court itself had made possible.
memory_variants.situation: The settlement could restore obedience widely — but every prince and exile excluded from it remained useful to France or to Sweden.

title: The Amnesty Question
briefing: The Peace of Prague had drawn most of the Empire back to the emperor, but a few held out — and chief among them was Hessen-Kassel, which still had an army, foreign paymasters, and grievances. Its provisional acceptance of Prague would never become real obedience unless the terms were made real, and that meant deciding how far to bend.
situation: To press hard — demanding the Westphalian bishoprics, conceding little — would satisfy the Catholic claimants and Ferdinand's friends, but might reopen the war in the west.
