To concede enough would strike one armed enemy from the list, at the cost of teaching every holdout that defiance pays. It was the exclusion problem of Prague in miniature.
historian_note: Wilson treats Hessen-Kassel as a missed chance after Prague.

options.label: Hold the line, and let the deal fail if Hessen will not yield enough.
options.consequence: In the event, the terms could not be agreed, the ban followed, and Hessen-Kassel returned to the anti-imperial war with a sharpened grievance — one more client for France, exactly as the exclusions at Prague had threatened.

options.label: Offer security concessions to close the Hessen deal.
options.consequence: One dangerous army may be removed from the enemy's roll — but friends with claims in the region count the cost, and every other holdout notes that bargaining works.

options.label: Use military pressure to compel obedience.
options.consequence: The settlement speaks with cannon behind it. The war in the west hardens, and the line between pacifying the Empire and conquering it blurs further.

title: Regensburg Again
briefing: The succession Ferdinand had failed to secure at Regensburg in 1630 could wait no longer: the emperor's health was failing. With Nördlingen won and Prague signed, the electors were at last in a mood to oblige — but the price of their consent was a fresh set of restraints written into the bargain, the leverage they had guarded for seven years.
situation: To delay was to gamble the dynasty's future on the emperor's failing body. To press ahead was to accept that his son would inherit not only the crown but the conditions fastened to it. Every concession bought a smoother election; every restraint narrowed the throne his heir would sit on.
historian_note: Wilson treats Ferdinand III's election as dynastic success bound by consultation limits and unresolved war.

options.label: Secure Ferdinand III's election as King of the Romans.
options.consequence: In the event, the electors chose Ferdinand's son King of the Romans in 1636, and the dynasty outlived the emperor's body. The Habsburg succession was safe — but the war his son inherited would outlive the dynasty's success by another twelve years.

options.label: Buy warmer consent with broader procedural guarantees.
options.consequence: The election grows less brittle — and the crown less free, as the electors write their price into the constitution.

options.label: Delay the election until the military fortunes improve.
options.consequence: The chancery gains room to bargain and loses its sleep: every fever in the emperor's chamber now carries a constitutional meaning.

title: Credit Still Offered by the Estates
briefing: Even amid the war, some moderate estates signalled that they could still be worked with. Their message was conditional: imperial terms could be carried into their diets and assemblies — provided the old liberties were named and respected, not quietly swallowed.
situation: This was not affection but calculation: a belief, still alive, that obedience might protect privilege and confession better than armed resistance. Such credit was a wasting asset. Spent on a controlled settlement, it could keep more estates within reach; hoarded, it might be there later — or might curdle into the conviction that only force secures rights.
historian_note: Wilson repeatedly emphasizes that imperial government depended on cooperation by estates and princes, not command alone.

options.label: Spend the goodwill now: put the disputed claims before a controlled diet.
options.consequence: The court trades trust for procedure and keeps more estates reachable. The zealous councillors complain that law is being made slow just when victory should speak plainly.

options.label: Hold the goodwill in reserve for a later settlement.
options.consequence: A quarrel is avoided today, and the estates' confidence stays useful. But petitioners who hoped for action begin to read the delay as policy.

title: Guarantees Before Obedience
briefing: The petitions arriving now asked not for favour but for security in writing. Estates that had once merely disputed policy wanted to know what, after submission, would stop any privilege from being narrowed away — as the Letter of Majesty had been, as the Edict now threatened. They had learned to trust guarantees, not goodwill.
situation: In the climate the war had made, every concession looked like an admission of weakness, and every refusal strengthened the argument that only guarantees backed by arms could protect a liberty. Ferdinand could offer written security while preserving obedience in form, or insist that obedience must come first and privilege after.
historian_note: The game abstracts Wilson's wider constitutional point: fear of overreach made settlement harder even after imperial victories.

options.label: Offer written guarantees while preserving obedience in form.
options.consequence: Some moderates get language they can carry home and defend. The Catholic hardliners and the victorious officers hear that rebellion has taught the court to bargain — and file the lesson away.

options.label: Refuse guarantees; insist obedience precede every privilege.
options.consequence: The court keeps the order of authority intact. The petitions go home unanswered — and the foreign patrons gain one more file of grievances to wave.

title: Arrears on Every Table
briefing: The armies that won the war could not be paid for it. Pay fell into arrears across every command — colonels, creditors, and allied agents arriving with the same unmet accounts in different hands. Soldiers could be promised discipline, but not fed on promises; and an unpaid army was a danger to friend and foe alike.
situation: The question before the council was no longer how to finance a policy, but which policy could survive the arrears. Ferdinand could lean harder on the contribution system — making the occupied lands pay — or shrink the army to save its core and its credit.
historian_note: Wilson treats war finance and contribution systems as central to the war's political escalation.

options.label: Lean on contributions until pay can be restored.
options.consequence: The army keeps the field by squeezing the lands harder. Every requisition makes the emperor's war visible in barn, cellar, and town account — and turns more subjects into enemies.

options.label: Disband the unreliable companies and save credit for the core army.
options.consequence: The treasury breathes a little. The commanders protest, the allies doubt the army's reach, and the crown accepts a smaller instrument for a steadier one.

title: Ready Money, Rare Freedom
briefing: For once the treasury could answer a demand without surrendering land, title, or command in place of coin. It was not rich — but it had ready money, and ready money bought something victory alone did not: the freedom to say no.
situation: A crown that could pay its servants need not make them princes. Ferdinand could spend the credit to keep military rewards within ordinary bounds — sparing the constitution another Mecklenburg — or hoard it for the succession and the diplomacy ahead, and let the commanders wait their turn behind dynastic business.
historian_note: This is a game abstraction from Wilson's emphasis on the political power created by fiscal scarcity.

options.label: Spend ready credit to keep rewards within ordinary grants.
options.consequence: Officers grumble less when paid, and fewer servants need to be made princes. The treasury buys constitutional quiet at a real and recurring cost.

options.label: Reserve the credit for the succession and diplomacy.
options.consequence: The court keeps its money for the next great bargain — and the commanders note that their accounts stand second to the business of the dynasty.

title: The Price of Armed Servants
briefing: The men who kept armies in the field now sent counsel along with their accounts. Contractors, colonels, and allied commanders — the Wallensteins and the Bavarians on whom the war depended — wanted to know whether policy would follow the soldiers who made policy possible. An army raised on credit and contribution answered, in the end, to whoever paid it.
situation: To refuse these creditors risked the very instrument of survival; to satisfy them taught every prince that imperial necessity could be made to pay. The emperor could buy their loyalty before it curdled into rivalry, or reassert that credit was not sovereignty and dare the consequences.
historian_note: This abstracts the recurring Bavarian and Wallenstein problem: military capacity could become leverage over imperial policy.

options.label: Satisfy the armed creditors before they become rivals.
options.consequence: The army stays usable — but obedience bought in open view becomes a precedent, and the price of survival is paid again every campaign.

options.label: Reassert command and risk a breach with the military creditors.
options.consequence: The court reminds its servants that credit is not sovereignty. The reminder is lawful, dangerous, and ruinous if the army hesitates at the wrong moment.

date_label: When foreign intervention risk is extreme
title: Foreign Courts Find Their Cause
briefing: The reports from abroad carried a new and ominous note. Imperial quarrels were being translated, in Stockholm and Paris, into the language of the European balance — of protection owed, of recovery deserved, of religion in danger. What Vienna called domestic law, other crowns were beginning to call a continental threat.
situation: Ferdinand could still insist the war was an internal matter of the Empire. But Sweden was in Germany and France was edging toward it, and every assertion of imperial power abroad read as a reason to intervene. He could answer with public reassurances that denied the foreign courts their pretext, or with a decisive blow that might silence them — or prove them right.
historian_note: Wilson frames the widening war as a fusion of imperial settlement, dynastic security, and foreign-policy calculation.

options.label: Send public reassurances to deny the foreign courts their pretext.
options.consequence: The papers make intervention harder to justify — but they also bind the emperor to words that allies and estates will quote back at him when he wants to act.

options.label: Answer foreign pressure with a decisive military demonstration.
options.consequence: A victory might silence patrons and clients together. A defeat would prove to all Europe that the Empire has become its battlefield — and invite everyone in.

title: A Crown Not Yet in Panic
briefing: For a rare interval, the succession did not have to be bought in the same breath as every military demand. With his son's position more secure, Ferdinand had room — a thing war seldom allows — to choose which concessions to make and which to keep.
situation: Security could make moderation easier, freeing the court to settle from confidence rather than fear. It could as easily tempt it to spend less on settlement, the dynasty itself being safe. The breathing space was an asset that could be invested in peace or hoarded for the house.
historian_note: This is the reward side of Ferdinand's dynastic problem: security changes what concessions are politically bearable.

options.label: Use the dynasty's security to offer wider settlement terms.
options.consequence: The court can concede without sounding desperate. The Catholic allies complain — but some estates hear strength rather than retreat, and edge back toward obedience.

options.label: Guard the dynasty's security and make fewer promises.
options.consequence: The house stays safer — but the Empire hears less of reconciliation and more of continuity, and the dissatisfied keep their distance.

title: The Lands Petition Against Ruin
briefing: The petitions no longer separated grand strategy from hunger. Town councils, district officers, and church administrators wrote of fields unsown, villages emptied, soldiers quartered without end, and contributions that could not be paid because there was nothing left to take. The war's cost had moved from the ledger into the body of the land.
situation: Devastation had become an argument in council itself: even loyal men now asked what obedience could mean if the lands that obeyed were consumed. Ferdinand could order relief and cap contributions in the worst-hit regions, or keep the contributions flowing until peace was nearer and trust the land to endure.
historian_note: Wilson treats wartime devastation and material exhaustion as political facts, not merely background suffering.

options.label: Order relief and contribution limits in the worst-hit lands.
options.consequence: The order gives loyal estates words to defend obedience with. The commanders answer that armies cannot march on mercy, and that an unfed soldier feeds himself.

options.label: Keep contributions flowing until peace is nearer.
options.consequence: The army stays supplied, and the petitions grow darker. Peace itself begins to look like the only relief anyone still believes in.

title: The Emperor Dies
briefing: On 15 February 1637 Ferdinand II died in Vienna, in his bed, the succession secured and his faith triumphant in the hereditary lands. He had taken a provincial archduke's crown and made himself master of a recatholicized Austria and Bohemia, broken the Bohemian and Palatine revolts, and outlived the Swedish thunderbolt. By the measure of his own beginnings, he had won.
situation: And yet the war he had done so much to start, and to widen, did not end with him. Every unsettled question passed to his son, Ferdinand III: the half-kept amnesty, the unpaid armies, the foreign crowns now lodged in the Empire, the devastated lands, and the deepest question of all — how much imperial authority the Empire could bear before cooperation broke for good. The memorial of the reign now had to be closed.
historian_note: Wilson marks Ferdinand II's death as dynastic continuity amid unresolved amnesty, fiscal, foreign, and military problems.

options.label: Receive the final memorial of the reign.
options.consequence: The record is sealed for the next emperor. Ferdinand's victories were real; so were the wars they did not end. He died believing the worst was over. It was not: the war would grind on until 1648, and the Peace of Westphalia would settle it on terms closer to his enemies' than his own.

options.label: Order a final summary of the settlement for Ferdinand III.
options.consequence: The clerks gather the unsettled questions into a single inheritance: authority, confession, debt, armies, and a peace still eleven years away.
